subject: Combined Science B (Twenty First Century Science)

units.title: Chapter B1: You and your genes

topics.title: B1.1 What is the genome and what does it do?

outcomes.text: Explain how the nucleus, plasmids and other genetic material relate to the functions of eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells.
Describe how to use a light microscope to observe a variety of plant and animal cells.
Describe the genome as all the genetic material of an organism.
Describe DNA as a polymer of nucleotides forming two strands in a double helix.
Explain the terms chromosome, gene, allele, variant, genotype and phenotype.
Describe simply how the genome and the environment together shape an organism's phenotype.
Explain why amino acids matter in making proteins, with the genome as instructions for joining them.

topics.title: B1.2 How is genetic information inherited?

outcomes.text: Explain the terms gamete, homozygous, heterozygous, dominant and recessive.
Explain single gene inheritance, including dominant and recessive alleles and genetic diagrams.
Predict the results of single gene crosses.
Use direct proportions and simple ratios in genetic crosses.
Use probability to predict the outcome of genetic crosses.
Recall that most features result from multiple genes rather than a single gene.
Describe how sex is determined in humans.

topics.title: B1.3 How can and should gene technology be used?

outcomes.text: Discuss why understanding the human genome matters for medicine, including disease-linked alleles and genetic testing for family planning and healthcare.
Describe genetic engineering as modifying an organism's genome to introduce desirable characteristics.
Describe the main steps of genetic engineering: isolating the gene, putting it in a vector, inserting it into cells, selecting modified cells.

subtopics.title: Benefits and risks of gene technology

outcomes.text: Explain benefits and risks, practical and ethical, of gene technology in agriculture and medicine.

topics.title: B2.1 What are the causes of disease?

outcomes.text: Describe the relationship between health and disease.
Describe different types of disease, including communicable and non-communicable.
Explain how communicable diseases caused by viruses, bacteria, protists and fungi spread in animals and plants.
Describe common human infections: influenza, Salmonella, athlete's foot, malaria, and sexually transmitted infections including HIV/AIDS.
Describe plant diseases: tobacco mosaic virus, ash dieback and crown gall disease.

topics.title: B2.2 How do organisms protect themselves against pathogens?

outcomes.text: Describe non-specific defences against pathogens, with physical, chemical and microbial examples.
Explain how platelets are adapted to their function in the blood.
Explain the role of the immune system in defence against disease.
Explain how white blood cells are adapted to their functions and how this protects against disease.

topics.title: B2.3 How can we prevent the spread of infection?

outcomes.text: Explain how the spread of communicable diseases can be reduced in animals and plants, using human infection, plant disease and STI examples.
Explain how vaccines prevent disease, using safe forms of pathogens, and why a large share of the population must be vaccinated.

topics.title: B2.4 How can lifestyle, genes and the environment affect health?

outcomes.text: Describe how genetic and lifestyle factors together raise or lower the risk of non-communicable diseases.
Describe how to investigate the effect of exercise on pulse rate and recovery rate.
Use data to explain how common non-communicable diseases are locally, nationally and globally in relation to exercise, diet, alcohol and smoking.
Translate disease data between graphs and numbers.
Construct and interpret frequency tables, bar charts and histograms.
Understand the principles of sampling in scientific data.
Use a scatter diagram to identify a correlation between two variables.
Describe interactions between different types of disease.

topics.title: B2.5 How can we treat disease?

outcomes.text: Explain the use of medicines in treating disease.
Calculate cross-sectional areas of bacterial cultures and clear zones around antibiotic discs using pi r squared.
Evaluate strategies for lowering the risk of and treating cardiovascular disease: lifestyle, medicines and surgery.
Describe how new medicines are discovered and developed, including preclinical and clinical testing.

units.title: Chapter B3: Living together - food and ecosystems

topics.title: B3.1 What happens during photosynthesis?

outcomes.text: Describe photosynthesis, its two stages, their inputs and outputs, the need for light, and that it is endothermic.
Describe practical investigations into the requirements and products of photosynthesis.
Explain how chloroplasts in plant cells relate to photosynthesis.
Explain how enzymes work: active site, specificity, and how substrate concentration, temperature and pH change the rate.
Describe practical investigations into how substrate concentration, temperature and pH affect enzyme-controlled reactions.
Explain how temperature, light intensity and carbon dioxide concentration affect the rate of photosynthesis, and how to investigate this.
Use the inverse square law to explain how the rate changes with distance from a light source.
Explain how temperature, light and carbon dioxide interact in limiting photosynthesis, using graphs.
Use compound measures such as rate of reaction in photosynthesis contexts.
Translate photosynthesis data between graphs and numbers.
Plot graphs with suitable axis scales for photosynthesis data.
Extract and interpret information from graphs, charts and tables.

topics.title: B3.2 How do producers get the substances they need?

outcomes.text: Describe substances moving into and out of photosynthetic organisms, including oxygen, carbon dioxide, water and mineral ions.
Explain how substances cross cell membranes by diffusion, osmosis and active transport, and describe practicals on diffusion and osmosis.
Explain how partially permeable membranes of plant and prokaryotic cells relate to cell function.
Explain how roots take up water and mineral ions, relating root hair cell structure to function.
Explain how xylem and phloem are adapted to their functions, and how to observe them with a microscope.
Describe transpiration and translocation, stomata structure and function, and how to use a simple potometer.
Explain how light intensity, air movement and temperature affect water uptake, and how to investigate this.
Use compound measures and carry out rate calculations for water uptake.
Plot, draw and interpret graphs of water uptake.
Calculate percentage gain and loss of mass.

topics.title: B3.3 How are organisms in an ecosystem interdependent?

outcomes.text: Explain the importance of sugars, fatty acids, glycerol and amino acids in making and breaking down carbohydrates, lipids and proteins, and describe qualitative tests for biological molecules.
Describe photosynthetic organisms as the main producers of food and biomass on Earth.
Describe substances transported into organisms, including dissolved food molecules.
Describe the levels of organisation in an ecosystem from individuals to the whole ecosystem.
Explain the importance of interdependence and competition in a community.
Recall that many substances cycle between the biotic and abiotic parts of an ecosystem.
Explain the importance of the carbon cycle and water cycle to living organisms.
Explain the role of microorganisms in cycling substances through an ecosystem.
Calculate percentage of mass in the use and cycling of substances in ecosystems.

topics.title: B3.4 How are populations affected by the conditions in an ecosystem?

outcomes.text: Explain how abiotic and biotic factors affect communities, including toxic chemicals, food, predators and pathogens.
Describe a field investigation into the distribution and abundance of organisms and how to estimate numbers in an area.
Calculate arithmetic means for population data.
Understand and use percentiles.
Plot graphs with suitable scales for population data.
Extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables.

units.title: Chapter B4: Using food and controlling growth

topics.title: B4.1 What happens during cellular respiration?

outcomes.text: Compare aerobic and anaerobic respiration: conditions, inputs, outputs and ATP yield.
Explain why cellular respiration occurs continuously in all living cells.
Explain how mitochondria relate to cellular respiration.
Describe cellular respiration as an exothermic process.
Describe investigations into how substrates affect the rate of respiration in yeast.
Carry out rate calculations for respiration.

topics.title: B4.2 How do we know about mitochondria and other cell structures?

outcomes.text: Explain how electron microscopy has increased our understanding of sub-cellular structures.
Understand number, size and scale and the relationships between units for cells and sub-cellular structures.
Use estimations and explain when to use them.
Calculate with numbers in standard form.

topics.title: B4.3 How do organisms grow and develop?

outcomes.text: Describe the cell cycle's role in growth, including interphase and mitosis, and how to observe mitosis with a microscope.
Describe cancer as changes in cells causing uncontrolled growth and division.
Explain how meiosis halves the chromosome number to form gametes.
Describe the function of stem cells in embryonic and adult animals and meristems in plants.
Explain why cell differentiation matters: cells specialise by switching genes on and off.

topics.title: B4.4 Should we use stem cells to treat damage and disease?

outcomes.text: Discuss benefits, risks and ethical issues of using stem cells in medicine.

units.title: Chapter B5: The human body - staying alive

topics.title: B5.1 How do substances get into, out of and around our bodies?

outcomes.text: Describe substances moving into and out of the human body to meet cell needs: oxygen, carbon dioxide, water, food molecules and urea.
Explain how partially permeable animal cell membranes relate to diffusion, osmosis and active transport.
Describe the human circulatory system and its links with the gaseous exchange, digestive and excretory systems.
Explain how the heart's structure, including cardiac muscle, chambers and valves, suits its function.
Explain how arteries, veins and capillaries are adapted to their functions.
Explain how red blood cells and plasma are adapted to their functions.
Explain the need for exchange surfaces and a transport system in terms of surface area to volume ratio.
Calculate surface area to volume ratios.

topics.title: B5.2 How does the nervous system help us respond to changes?

outcomes.text: Explain how receptors, sensory neurons, the CNS, motor neurons and effectors work together.
Explain how the structures of nerve cells and synapses relate to their functions.
Explain how a reflex arc, including the relay neuron, suits its function, and describe reflex investigations.

topics.title: B5.3 How do hormones control responses in the human body?

outcomes.text: Describe how the endocrine system coordinates and controls the body with hormones.
Explain the roles of thyroxine and adrenaline, with thyroxine as an example of negative feedback.

topics.title: B5.4 Why do we need to maintain a constant internal environment?

outcomes.text: Explain why a constant internal environment matters in response to internal and external change.
Extract and interpret data from graphs, charts and tables on internal environment control.
Translate information between numerical and graphical forms.

topics.title: B5.5 What role do hormones play in human reproduction?

outcomes.text: Describe the role of hormones in human reproduction, including control of the menstrual cycle.
Explain how FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone interact to control the menstrual cycle.
Explain hormones in contraception and evaluate hormonal and non-hormonal methods.
Explain the use of hormones in reproductive technologies to treat infertility.

topics.title: B5.6 What can happen when organs and control systems stop working?

outcomes.text: Explain how insulin controls blood sugar level.
Explain how glucagon and insulin work together to control blood sugar.
Compare type 1 and type 2 diabetes and explain how each is treated.

units.title: Chapter B6: Life on Earth - past, present and future

topics.title: B6.1 How was the theory of evolution developed?

outcomes.text: State that there is usually extensive genetic variation within a species population.
Recall that genetic variants arise from mutations and that most have no effect on phenotype.
Explain how natural selection favours variants giving phenotypes better suited to the environment.
Explain the importance of competition in a community for natural selection.
Describe evolution as change in inherited characteristics of a population over generations, possibly forming new species.
Explain the impact of selective breeding of food plants and domesticated animals.
Describe how fossils provide evidence for evolution.
Describe modern evidence for evolution, including antibiotic resistance in bacteria.

topics.title: B6.2 How does our understanding of biology help us classify the diversity of organisms on Earth?

outcomes.text: Describe how developments in biology, including DNA analysis, have changed classification systems.

topics.title: B6.3 Why is biodiversity threatened and how can we protect it?

outcomes.text: Describe positive and negative human interactions with ecosystems and their impact on biodiversity.
Explain benefits and challenges of maintaining local and global biodiversity.
Extract and interpret biodiversity information from charts, graphs and tables.

topics.title: C1.1 How has the Earth's atmosphere changed over time, and why?

outcomes.text: Explain the particle model for states of matter and changes of state, and tell physical from chemical changes.
Explain the limitations of the particle model when particles are drawn as inelastic spheres.
Use energy transfers and strength of forces between particles to explain why changes of state occur at different temperatures.
Use data to predict the states of substances under given conditions.
Interpret evidence for how the atmosphere was originally formed.
Describe how an oxygen-rich atmosphere developed over time.
Describe sources of carbon monoxide, particulates, sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides.
Explain problems from these pollutants and ways to cut emissions: catalytic converters, low sulfur petrol, gas scrubbers.
Use chemical symbols to write formulae of elements and simple covalent compounds.
Write formulae and balanced chemical equations using conservation of mass.
Use arithmetic and ratios when balancing equations.
Describe tests to identify oxygen, hydrogen and carbon dioxide.
Explain oxidation as gain of oxygen.

topics.title: C1.2 Why are there temperature changes in chemical reactions?

outcomes.text: Tell endothermic from exothermic reactions by the temperature change of the surroundings.
Draw and label reaction profiles for exothermic and endothermic reactions, showing activation energy.
Explain activation energy as the energy needed for a reaction to occur.
Interpret charts and graphs of reaction profiles.
Calculate energy changes in a reaction from bond breaking and bond making energies.
Carry out the arithmetic when calculating energy changes.

topics.title: C1.3 What is the evidence for climate change, why is it occurring?

outcomes.text: Describe the greenhouse effect in terms of radiation interacting with matter.
Evaluate evidence for human causes of climate change, such as carbon dioxide rising with fossil fuel use, and its uncertainties.
Describe effects of more carbon dioxide and methane on climate: crop areas, extreme weather, melting ice and flooding.
Describe how these effects may be mitigated, considering scale, risk and environmental impact.
Extract and interpret information from charts, graphs and tables.
Use orders of magnitude to judge the significance of data.

topics.title: C1.4 How can scientists help improve the supply of potable water?

outcomes.text: Describe the main methods of increasing potable water: filtration, membrane filtration, aeration, bacteria, chlorination and distillation.
Describe a test to identify chlorine using blue litmus paper.

topics.title: C2.1 How have our ideas about atoms developed over time?

outcomes.text: Describe how and why the atomic model changed through Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr.
Describe the atom as a positive nucleus surrounded by electrons, with most mass in a very small nucleus.
Recall relative charges and approximate relative masses of protons, neutrons and electrons.
Estimate the size and scale of atoms relative to other particles.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Relate the size and scale of atoms to objects in the physical world.
Calculate numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons from atomic and mass numbers or the Periodic Table.

topics.title: C2.2 What does the Periodic Table tell us about elements?

outcomes.text: Explain how an element's position relates to its electron arrangement and atomic number.
Describe how Mendeleev organised elements by properties and relative atomic masses.
Describe how new elements and ordering by atomic number supported Mendeleev's gaps and reordering.
Describe and explain differences between metals and non-metals in physical and chemical properties.
Recall simple properties of Group 1 elements, including reactions with moist air, water and chlorine.
Describe experiments to find the reactivity pattern of Group 1 elements.
Recall simple properties of Group 7 elements: states, colours, reactions with Group 1 and displacement reactions.
Describe experiments to find the reactivity pattern of Group 7 elements, including displacement.
Predict reactions and likely reactivity of elements from their Periodic Table positions.

topics.title: C2.3 How do metals and non-metals combine to form compounds?

outcomes.text: Recall simple properties of Group 0: low melting and boiling points, gases, unreactive.
Explain how properties of Groups 1, 7 and 0 depend on outer electrons, and predict properties from trends.
Explain how element reactions relate to electron arrangement and atomic number.
Explain how the atomic structure of metals and non-metals relates to their Periodic Table position.
Describe the nature and arrangement of chemical bonds in ionic compounds.
Explain ionic bonding in terms of electrostatic forces and electron transfer.
Calculate numbers of protons, neutrons and electrons in atoms and ions.
Construct dot and cross diagrams for simple ionic substances.
Explain how bulk properties of ionic materials relate to their bonds.
Use energy transfers and strength of attraction between ions to explain melting points of ionic compounds.
Describe limitations of dot and cross diagrams and 3-D representations of ions and ionic compounds.
Translate between diagrammatic and numerical forms and between 3-D and 2-D representations of ionic structures.

topics.title: C2.4 How are equations used to represent chemical reactions?

outcomes.text: Use chemical symbols to write formulae of elements and simple covalent and ionic compounds.
Use common ion formulae to deduce formulae of Group 1 and Group 7 compounds.
Write formulae and balanced equations using the first 20 elements, Groups 1, 7 and 0 and common elements.
Describe physical states using state symbols (s, l, g and aq).

units.title: Chapter C3: Chemicals of the natural environment

topics.title: C3.1 How are the atoms held together in a metal?

outcomes.text: Describe the nature and arrangement of chemical bonds in metals.
Explain how bulk properties of metals relate to their bonds.

topics.title: C3.2 How are metals with different reactivities extracted?

outcomes.text: Deduce an order of reactivity of metals from reactions with water, acid and other metals.
Explain how reactivity with water or acid relates to the tendency to form positive ions.
Write formulae, balanced equations and ionic equations using conservation of mass.
Explain how carbon's place in the reactivity series determines industrial metal extraction, including zinc.
Explain why electrolysis is used to extract some metals from their ores.
Evaluate biological methods of metal extraction: bacterial and phytoextraction.

topics.title: C3.3 What are electrolytes and what happens during electrolysis?

outcomes.text: Describe electrolysis in terms of the ions present and reactions at the electrodes.
Predict products of electrolysis of molten binary ionic compounds.
Recall that metals or hydrogen form at the cathode and non-metals at the anode with inert electrodes.
Write half equations for electrolysis.
Explain reduction and oxidation as gain or loss of electrons.
Explain how electrolysis extracts metals from ores, including aluminium.
Describe competing reactions in electrolysis of aqueous ionic solutions, including oxygen, chlorine, metals and hydrogen.
Describe the technique for electrolysis of an aqueous salt solution.

topics.title: C3.4 Why is crude oil important as a source of new materials?

outcomes.text: Recall that crude oil is a main source of hydrocarbons and a feedstock for the petrochemical industry.
Explain how modern life depends on hydrocarbons and that crude oil is finite.
Describe and explain separating crude oil by fractional distillation.
Describe the fractions as mainly alkanes of formula CnH2n+2 in the alkane homologous series.
Use energy transfers and strength of bonds and intermolecular forces to explain different state-change temperatures.
Deduce the empirical formula of a compound from atom numbers, a model or a diagram, and vice versa.
Use arithmetic and ratio to determine empirical formulae.
Describe the arrangement of chemical bonds in simple molecules.
Explain covalent bonding as sharing of electrons.
Construct dot and cross diagrams for simple covalent substances.
Represent three-dimensional shapes in two dimensions and vice versa for simple molecules.
Describe limitations of dot and cross diagrams, ball and stick models and 2-D/3-D representations.
Translate information between diagrammatic and numerical forms.

subtopics.title: Properties of simple molecules and cracking

outcomes.text: Explain how bulk properties of simple molecules relate to covalent bonds and intermolecular forces.
Describe how cracking makes more useful materials.

topics.title: C4.1 How is data used to choose a material for a particular use?

outcomes.text: Compare quantitatively the physical properties of glass and clay ceramics, polymers, composites and metals.
Explain how material properties relate to uses and select suitable materials for a given use.

topics.title: C4.2 How do bonding and structure affect properties of materials?

outcomes.text: Explain how bulk properties relate to bond types, bond strengths versus intermolecular forces, and bond arrangement.
Describe and compare bonding and arrangement in ionic compounds, simple molecules, giant covalent structures, polymers and metals.
Recall that carbon can form four covalent bonds.
Explain how carbon's chains and rings give a vast array of organic compounds in families.
Describe bonding in polymers and how it affects strength, flexibility, hardness and melting point.
Describe the nature and arrangement of bonds in giant covalent structures.
Explain properties of diamond and graphite from their structures and bonding.
Represent 3-D structures such as carbon allotropes in two dimensions and vice versa.

topics.title: C4.3 Why are nanoparticles so useful?

outcomes.text: Compare nano dimensions with typical dimensions of atoms and molecules.
Describe how surface area to volume ratio changes with particle size and how this affects properties.
Describe how nanoparticle properties relate to their uses.
Explain the properties of fullerenes and graphene from their structures.
Explain possible risks of nanoparticles, including health effects, data gaps and relative risks and benefits.
Estimate the size and scale of atoms and nanoparticles, including the 1 to 100 nanometre range.
Interpret, order and calculate with numbers in standard form for nanoparticles.
Use ratios for relative sizes and surface area to volume comparisons.
Calculate surface areas and volumes of cubes.

topics.title: C4.4 What happens to products at the end of their useful life?

outcomes.text: Explain reduction and oxidation as loss or gain of oxygen, identifying what is oxidised and reduced.
Explain reduction and oxidation as gain or loss of electrons.
Describe the basic principles of a life-cycle assessment, including water, energy, disposal routes and biodegradability.
Interpret data from a life-cycle assessment.
Describe how PET drinks bottles are reused and recycled, and why this is viable.
Evaluate factors affecting decisions on recycling products from crude oil and metal ores.

topics.title: C5.1 How are chemicals separated and tested for purity?

outcomes.text: Explain that many useful materials are formulations of mixtures.
Explain purity, distinguishing scientific from everyday use of 'pure'.
Use melting point data to tell pure from impure substances.
Recall that chromatography uses a stationary and mobile phase and separation depends on distribution between them.
Interpret chromatograms, including calculating Rf values.
Suggest chromatographic methods to tell pure from impure substances.
Describe, explain and exemplify filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation and fractional distillation.
Suggest suitable purification techniques from information about substances.

topics.title: C5.2 How are the amounts of substances in reactions calculated?

outcomes.text: Recall and use the law of conservation of mass.
Explain apparent mass changes in non-enclosed systems using the particle model.

subtopics.title: Relative formula mass and the mole

outcomes.text: Calculate relative formula masses of species and in a balanced equation.
Recall and use the Avogadro constant and the mole.
Explain and use the link between mass in grams and amount in moles.
Carry out calculations with the Avogadro constant in standard form.
Change the subject of a mathematical equation.
Deduce the stoichiometry of an equation from masses and explain the effect of a limiting reactant.
Use a balanced equation to calculate masses of reactants or products.
Use arithmetic, ratio, percentage and multistep calculations throughout quantitative chemistry.

topics.title: C5.3 How are the amounts of chemicals in solution measured?

outcomes.text: Explain and calculate concentration in g/dm3 from mass of solute and volume.
Explain and calculate concentration in mol/dm3 from moles of solute and volume.
Describe neutralisation as acid plus alkali giving salt and water, for common laboratory acids and alkalis.
Recall that acids form hydrogen ions in water and alkali solutions contain hydroxide ions.
Recognise that neutralisation is hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to form water.
Describe and explain the titration procedure for precise, accurate, valid and repeatable results.
Evaluate the quality of titration data.

topics.title: C6.1 What useful products can be made from acids?

outcomes.text: Recall that acids react with some metals and carbonates, and write equations predicting products.
Describe practical procedures to make salts using filtration, evaporation, crystallisation and drying.
Use formulae of common ions to deduce the formula of a compound.
Recall that acidity and alkalinity are measured by pH, using universal indicator and pH meters.
Use and explain dilute, concentrated, weak and strong for acids, including differences in reactivity.
Use the idea that a tenfold rise in hydrogen ion concentration lowers pH by one.
Describe neutrality, acidity and alkalinity in terms of hydrogen ion concentration and whole-number pH.

topics.title: C6.2 How do chemists control the rate of reactions?

outcomes.text: Describe the effect on reaction rate of temperature, concentration, pressure and surface area.
Explain effects of temperature, concentration and pressure through frequency and energy of particle collisions.
Explain the effect of piece size of a solid using surface area to volume ratio.
Describe the characteristics of catalysts and their effect on rate.
Identify catalysts in reactions.
Explain catalytic action in terms of activation energy.
Describe enzymes as catalysts in biological systems and some industrial processes.
Suggest practical methods for measuring a reaction's rate: gas volume, mass change, colour change, precipitate.
Interpret rate of reaction graphs.
Use arithmetic and ratios when measuring rates.
Draw and interpret graphs from data to find rate.
Determine gradients of graphs as a measure of rate.
Use proportionality when comparing factors affecting rate.

topics.title: C6.3 What factors affect the yield of chemical reactions?

outcomes.text: Recall that some reactions are reversible and, in closed systems, do not reach 100% yield.
Recall that dynamic equilibrium is when forward and reverse reaction rates are equal.
Predict how concentration, temperature and pressure change equilibrium position, and suggest suitable conditions, noting catalysts and extreme-condition drawbacks.

topics.title: P1.1 What are the risks and benefits of using radiations?

outcomes.text: Describe the groupings of the electromagnetic spectrum, from long to short wavelength, low to high frequency and energy.
Recall that our eyes detect only a limited range of electromagnetic frequencies.
Recall that all electromagnetic radiation travels through space at the same very high but finite speed.
Explain with examples that electromagnetic radiation transfers energy from source to absorber.
Recall that substances absorb, transmit or reflect radiation depending on wavelength.
Recall that electrons sit at different distances from the nucleus, can change levels by absorbing or emitting radiation, and atoms become ions by losing outer electrons.
Recall how changes in molecules, atoms and nuclei generate and absorb radiation, including ionisation and ozone absorbing ultraviolet.
Describe hazardous effects of ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays on body tissues.
Give practical examples of uses of each region of the electromagnetic spectrum.
Recall that radio waves are produced by, or induce, oscillations in electrical circuits.

topics.title: P1.2 What is climate change and what is the evidence for it?

outcomes.text: Explain that all bodies emit radiation whose intensity and wavelength depend on temperature.
Explain how a body's temperature depends on the balance of incoming, absorbed and emitted radiation, including factors setting Earth's temperature.

topics.title: P1.3 How do waves behave?

outcomes.text: Describe wave motion using amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period.
Describe evidence that in water ripples and sound, the wave travels rather than the medium.
Describe the difference between transverse and longitudinal waves.
Describe waves on a rope as transverse and sound waves in air as longitudinal.
Define wavelength and frequency.
Recall and apply wave speed = frequency x wavelength across all kinds of waves.
Describe how to measure the speed of ripples and sound, and use a ripple tank for speed, frequency and wavelength.
Describe reflection and refraction of waves at material interfaces and how to investigate them.
Recall that waves travel at different speeds in different substances, varying with wavelength.
Explain refraction in terms of differing wave speeds in different substances.
Recall that light is an electromagnetic wave and that electromagnetic waves are transverse.

topics.title: P2.1 How much energy do we use?

outcomes.text: Describe how energy in chemical stores is transferred by an electric current to do work in domestic devices.
Explain how power ratings, time of use and changes in stored energy are related.
Recall and apply energy transferred = power x time.
Describe energy transfers in a system and that total energy in a closed system does not change.
Describe examples where energy is dissipated into less useful stores.
Explain ways of reducing unwanted energy transfer, such as lubrication and thermal insulation.
Describe how wall thickness and thermal conductivity affect the cooling rate of a building.
Calculate efficiency as useful over total energy transferred, and describe ways to raise it.
Interpret and construct Sankey diagrams to show energy conservation.

topics.title: P2.2 How can electricity be generated?

outcomes.text: Describe main energy resources on Earth: fossil fuels, nuclear fuel, biofuel, wind, hydroelectricity, tides and the Sun.
Explain differences between renewable and non-renewable energy resources.
Compare how the main energy resources are used to generate electricity.

subtopics.title: Mains electricity and the National Grid

outcomes.text: Recall the UK supply is a.c. at 50 Hz and about 230 V, and explain direct versus alternating voltage.
Recall that National Grid transformers transfer power at high voltage and again at lower voltage locally.
Recall the functions and potential differences of live, neutral and earth wires and why a live wire is dangerous even with a switch open.
Explain patterns and trends in energy resource use in domestic, workplace and national contexts.

topics.title: P3.1 What determines the current in an electric circuit?

outcomes.text: Recall that current is rate of flow of charge, needs a potential difference and closed circuit, and is the same around a single loop.
Recall and use charge = current x time.
Recall that current depends on resistance and potential difference, and the units used.
Apply V = I x R in d.c. series circuits and describe an experiment on wire resistance.
Recall that some components have constant resistance while others change with current.
Use graphs to tell linear from non-linear elements and describe I-V experiments on lamps, diodes, LDRs and thermistors.
Represent circuits with standard symbols and conventions.

topics.title: P3.2 How do series and parallel circuits work?

outcomes.text: Relate potential difference to the work done per unit charge between two points.
Describe the differences between series and parallel circuits for current and potential difference, and investigate bulb brightness.
Explain why resistors in series increase and in parallel decrease net resistance.
Solve problems for series resistors using equivalent resistance.
Explain the design and use of d.c. series circuits for measurement, including lamps, diodes, thermistors and LDRs.

topics.title: P3.3 What determines the rate of energy transfer in a circuit?

outcomes.text: Describe energy transfers when a current does work on a component.
Explain how power relates to energy transferred over time.
Recall and use energy transferred = charge x potential difference.
Apply power = V x I and power = I squared x R.
Use energy conservation to show a step-up transformer lowers current, and use Vp x Ip = Vs x Is.
Explain why transmitting power at high voltage is more efficient.

topics.title: P3.4 What are magnetic fields?

outcomes.text: Describe attraction and repulsion between like and unlike poles of permanent magnets.
Describe a magnet's field and how strength and direction change from point to point.
Explain how a compass shows the Earth's core must be magnetic.
Describe the difference between permanent and induced magnets.
Describe how to show a current creates a magnetic effect.
Describe the pattern and direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire.
Recall that field strength depends on current and distance from the conductor.
Explain how the magnetic effect of a solenoid can be increased.

topics.title: P3.5 How do electric motors work?

outcomes.text: Describe the interaction forces between a magnet and a current-carrying conductor using magnetic fields.
Show that Fleming's left-hand rule gives the relative directions of force, conductor and field.
Apply force = flux density x current x length to calculate forces.
Explain how the force on a conductor causes rotation of the coil in a simple electric motor.

topics.title: P4.1 What are forces?

outcomes.text: Recall and apply Newton's third law.
Recall ways objects interact: gravity, electrostatics, magnetism and contact, including normal contact force and friction.
Describe how gravitational, electrostatic, magnetic and contact forces involve pairs of objects each feeling a force.
Represent interaction forces as vectors.
Define weight.
Describe how weight is measured.
Recall and apply weight = mass x gravitational field strength.

topics.title: P4.2 How can we describe motion?

outcomes.text: Recall and apply average speed = distance / time.
Recall typical speeds of wind, sound, walking, running, cycling and transport.
Measure distances and times to calculate speeds, and investigate a trolley down a ramp.
Convert units using ratios, including between m/s and km/h.
Explain the vector-scalar distinction for displacement and distance, velocity and speed.
Recall and apply acceleration = change in speed / time, and how to investigate acceleration.
Select and apply (final speed) squared - (initial speed) squared = 2 x acceleration x distance.
Recall the value of acceleration in free fall and calculate everyday accelerations from estimates.
Draw and use distance and speed against time graphs to find speeds and accelerations.
Interpret distance-time and velocity-time graphs, relating lines and slopes to motion.
Interpret enclosed areas in velocity-time graphs.

topics.title: P4.3 What is the connection between forces and motion?

outcomes.text: Describe the forces acting on an isolated solid object or system.
Describe using free body diagrams how several forces give a resultant force, including balanced forces.
Use scale vector diagrams to show the resolution of forces for a net force or equilibrium.
Recall and apply momentum = mass x velocity and describe conservation of momentum in collisions.
Apply Newton's second law: change in momentum = resultant force x time.
Apply Newton's first law to motion at uniform velocity and motion with changing speed or direction.
Explain that circular orbit motion has constant speed but changing velocity.
Explain inertial mass as force over acceleration.
Recall and apply force = mass x acceleration.
Use equations linking force, mass, velocity, acceleration and momentum to explain relationships.
Explain methods of measuring human reaction times and recall typical results.
Explain factors affecting a vehicle's stopping distance in emergencies and the safety implications.
Explain the dangers of large decelerations.

topics.title: P4.4 How can we describe motion in terms of energy transfers?

outcomes.text: Describe energy transfers when forces raise an object or move it along the line of the force.
Recall and apply work done = force x distance along the line of the force.
Recall and calculate kinetic energy = half x mass x speed squared.
Recall and calculate gravitational potential energy = mass x field strength x height.
Calculate energy transfers for changes in a system, using the relevant mechanical equations.
Calculate stored energy and transfers and convert between newton metres and joules.
Describe energy store changes in common situations: projectile, collision, accelerating object, slowing vehicle.
Explain power as the rate of energy transfer, with examples.
Recall and apply power = energy transferred / time.

topics.title: P5.1 What is radioactivity?

outcomes.text: Describe the atom as a positive nucleus surrounded by electrons, with the nucleus tiny and holding almost all the mass.
Describe how and why the atomic model changed through Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr.
Recall the typical size of atoms and small molecules.
Recall that nuclei contain protons and neutrons and that each element's nucleus has a characteristic positive charge.
Recall that isotopes are nuclei of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
Use conventional notation to show differences between isotopes.
Recall that unstable nuclei may emit alpha particles, beta particles, neutrons and gamma rays.
Relate emissions to changes in the nucleus's mass or charge.
Write balanced equations for alpha, beta, gamma and neutron emission.
Explain half-life and how it relates to the random nature of decay.
Calculate the decline in emission, as a ratio, after a whole number of half-lives.
Interpret activity-time graphs to find half-life.

topics.title: P5.2 How can radioactive materials be used safely?

outcomes.text: Recall the differences in penetration of alpha particles, beta particles and gamma rays.
Recall the differences between contamination and irradiation and compare their hazards.
Explain how ionising radiation can harm body tissues.
Explain why hazards differ with the radiation emitted and half-life.
Describe uses of nuclear radiation for imaging internal organs and for destroying unwanted tissue.

units.title: Chapter P6: Matter - models and explanations

topics.title: P6.1 How does energy transform matter?

outcomes.text: Define density and describe how to find the densities of solid and liquid objects.
Recall and apply density = mass / volume.
Describe energy transfers when a system is changed by heating, in terms of temperature change and specific heat capacity.
Define specific heat capacity and distinguish it from specific latent heat.
Apply change in internal energy = mass x specific heat capacity x temperature change, and explain safe apparatus use.
Apply energy for change of state = mass x specific latent heat.
Describe energy store changes when a system changes and its temperature rises.
Calculate energy transfers for temperature changes using mechanical, electrical and thermal equations.

topics.title: P6.2 How does the particle model explain the effects of heating?

outcomes.text: Explain density differences between states of matter from the arrangement of atoms or molecules.
Use the particle model to show mass is conserved in melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation and sublimation, unlike chemical changes.
Use the particle model to describe how heating raises stored energy and temperature or causes changes of state.
Explain how molecular motion links a gas's temperature and pressure, including pressure against temperature at constant volume.

topics.title: P6.3 How does the particle model relate to materials under stress?

outcomes.text: Explain with examples that stretching, bending or compressing an object needs more than one force.
Use the particle model to explain the difference between elastic and plastic deformation.
Describe the force-extension relationship for a spring and how to measure it.
Describe the difference between linear and non-linear force-extension systems.
Recall and apply force = spring constant x extension.
Calculate work done stretching a spring from the area under a force-extension graph, and how to do so safely.
Apply energy stored = half x spring constant x extension squared.

topics.title: IaS1 What needs to be considered when investigating a phenomenon scientifically?

outcomes.text: Use scientific theories and tentative explanations to develop and justify hypotheses and predictions.
Suggest apparatus, materials and techniques, justifying choices by precision, accuracy and validity of data.
Recognise the importance of scientific quantities and how they are determined.
Identify factors to control and how to control them.
Suggest and justify a sample size or range of values to measure.
Plan experiments with clear, logically ordered strategies for observing, producing substances, testing hypotheses and collecting data.
Identify hazards in data collection and ways to minimise risk.
Use scientific vocabulary to communicate an investigation's rationale and methods in diagrams, graphs, numbers and symbols.

topics.title: IaS2 What processes are needed to draw conclusions from data?

outcomes.text: Present observations and data in appropriate formats.
Use SI units and IUPAC nomenclature when processing data.
Use prefixes and powers of ten for orders of magnitude.
Translate data from one form to another.
Interconvert units when processing data.
Use an appropriate number of significant figures.
Choose graph types, axes and scales, plot points, draw lines of best fit and show uncertainty.
Identify patterns, use range and mean, and read gradients and interpolated or extrapolated values from graphs.
Evaluate data for accuracy, precision, repeatability and reproducibility, find sources of error and decide on outliers.
Evaluate an experimental strategy, suggest improvements and further investigations.
Interpret data to draw reasoned conclusions using scientific vocabulary.
Explain how far data increase or decrease confidence in a prediction or hypothesis.

topics.title: IaS3 How are scientific explanations developed?

outcomes.text: Use ideas about correlation and cause to read correlations, separate them from cause-effect links and judge plausible mechanisms.
Describe and explain scientific theories that developed over time and were modified with new evidence.
Describe in outline the peer review process for new scientific claims.
Use representational, spatial, descriptive, computational and mathematical models to solve problems, predict and identify limitations.

topics.title: IaS4 How do science and technology impact society?

outcomes.text: Describe everyday examples and technologies that have made significant positive differences to people's lives.
Identify risks that arise from new scientific or technological advances.
For a situation, identify risks and benefits to groups, discuss action, explain risk acceptance and tell perceived from calculated risk.
Suggest why different decisions on the same issue may suit different personal, social, economic or environmental contexts.
Tell questions science can answer from those it cannot, and state ethical issues and differing views.
Explain why scientists should communicate their work to a range of audiences.
